title: Graduation Arcade
intro: Five rounds pulling together the whole course. Get them right first try to earn ⭐⭐⭐!

rounds.prompt: Both motors are commanded at the same speed, but the robot circles instead of driving straight. What's the likely fault category?
options: Wiring — one motor's leads are probably swapped
rounds.explain: If the commanded speeds truly match, a circle almost always traces back to a physically reversed motor connection.

rounds.prompt: A robot resets the instant its motors start spinning. What does this symptom point to?
options: A bug in the robot's Python code
A power-system issue — the motor's startup current spike sagging the shared voltage rail
rounds.explain: A working LED and correct logic elsewhere, paired with a motor-triggered reset, is a classic real-world power symptom, not a software bug.

rounds.prompt: In the arena, what does 'fewer ticks used to reach the goal' approximate?
options: A rough stand-in for time — a more direct, efficient program
rounds.explain: Each tick is a fixed simulated time step, so fewer of them to the goal is a fair proxy for a faster run.

rounds.prompt: Match each capstone card field to what part of the course it draws on.
rounds.explain: The capstone card is deliberately structured as a map of the whole course, one field at a time.

rounds.prompt: Why does the final assessment take the form of Part Hunt rather than a written test?
options: It's easier to build than a quiz
It matches the hands-on, interactive teaching style used throughout the entire course
Written tests are technically impossible in this format
rounds.explain: Every module favoured doing over reciting — the final exam stays consistent with that all the way through.
